pilot.summary: Three-player pod at Tom's, me on Edgar, Alex on Sauron, Tom on blue-black. Five vampires down by turn three off three mana spent, and the whole table made Markov the problem immediately — I ate multiple wipes and a stack of counters, and rebuilt in a turn or two every time. I did not cast Edgar until I had eight mana, which is my own mistake; when he landed it was the finisher, and Olivia's Wrath into a wide haste swing got Alex to 1. Tom countered Champion of Dusk and Bloodthirsty Conqueror, I needed one more vampire, and had nothing.

Five-player pod at Oliver's, second game of the night, seat 5. Mulliganed once and kept a two-land hand out of stubbornness — I knew at the time it should have gone back. Blood Artist and Bloodthirsty Conqueror landed early and a wipe with the drain online killed eleven creatures: every opponent lost 11, I gained 11, and I was around 50 to the table's 20. Then Ryan's recurring artifact and enchantment removal picked off Anointed Procession and the rest, I ran out of steam with vampires on board and nothing in hand, and Deflecting Swat and Teferi's Protection sat uncast all game because the mana was always spent on vampires.

Three-player pod at Alex's in Orinda, game two of four, me against Alex and Stuart. "Best-case opener and it did not matter" — two lands plus Sol Ring into a Talisman, four mana on turn one, Edgar down fast, Warleader's Call and the token-enters enchantments in place — and then Edgar was the only vampire I cast all game. Got Alex to 12 commander damage before he assembled blockers and he closed later with an oversized threat; I ran out of steam on card draw again. The conversation with Alex afterwards is the part that matters: the deck changes direction from swarm typal to lords and payoffs, tokens become the dig engine, and the token-conversion axis from 25 August is withdrawn.

Five-player pod at Oliver's, game three of three, first night on the twelve-swap list. Tom's Goblin Sharpshooter pinged my tokens and that fed the card-draw creatures, so I was running my engine off his removal. I resolved a big flyer that draws cards, brought Edgar down, then pivoted to Bloodletter of Aclazotz for the doubled damage and swung lethal into Alex to take him out. Tom tutored a two-card infinite and closed before my lethal resolved — a loss with Edgar dominating the board, and one I want on record as unsatisfying in a way that losing to a better board is not.

Four-player pod at Alex's, first of two games on the night: me on Edgar, Oliver on Vito mono-black vampires, Tom on Purphoros mono-red goblin ETB, Alex on an Azorius counters deck. Strong opener — Viscera Seer turn one off a swamp for the eminence token and its sac ability used early, never missed a land drop, Elspeth out, then Edgar off Ancient Tomb on turn five — and early vampires plus Edgar swinging held momentum all game; Oliver said afterwards he was always a turn behind. I went too all-in on Tom with Elspeth exposed, she got taken down, and Tom's Purphoros ETB pings finished the job before my lethal landed, about an hour in. The two lessons I wrote down: once a planeswalker is online, keep blockers up and protect the engine before pushing tempo; and Purphoros is the natural predator for mid-range aggro, so the deck needs targeted disruption in white.

read.what_it_does: On v1.1.0 it opens with the eminence token swarm and then gets paid when those bodies die. Tom's Goblin Sharpshooter pinged my tokens all game and that fed the pay-two-life draw creatures, so I was running my engine off his removal (004); the next game it was Viscera Seer turn one off a swamp for the token, Elspeth, then Edgar off Ancient Tomb on turn five, and early vampires plus Edgar swinging grew a board that held momentum all game (005). Combat is still how it actually threatens to close: the lethal was Bloodletter of Aclazotz for doubled damage into a wide Edgar swing that took Alex out (004), and in 005 the lethal was coming when Tom's pings got there first — both worth holding against engine.json's thesis that the two proven kill routes need no combat damage. On V1 the same opening built a wide board that then ran dry (001, 002, 003); on the current list it has not run dry in either game (004, 005).
read.how_it_plays: Fast and completely visible. Five vampires by turn three off three mana spent, and the whole table decided Edgar was the problem immediately (001, on V1 — the low curve and eminence are unchanged) — that is the price of the plan, not a surprise. On the current list it is the deck the table is chasing: Oliver said afterwards he was always a turn behind (005), and on board state Edgar was dominating (004). It absorbs an enormous amount — multiple wipes and a stack of counters in one game with a real board back in a turn or two every time (001) — and it was still among the last standing in a five-player pod (002). Where it ends up, on both current-list games, is ahead on board with lethal in sight and beaten by a clock the board cannot block: a tutored two-card infinite before my lethal resolved (004), Purphoros ETB pings before my lethal landed (005). On V1 the same shape ended on a counter on the refuel (001) or a wipe with nothing left in hand (002).
mindful_of: Pushing tempo with Elspeth exposed. I went too all-in on Tom, the planeswalker got taken down, and Purphoros's pings finished it before lethal landed (005). My own lesson from that night: once a planeswalker is online, keep blockers up and protect the engine before pushing tempo. Elspeth pulls removal every time she has shown up — targeted immediately on V1 too (001) — and she is still in the 99.

A Purphoros-style ETB deck is the natural predator for this mid-range aggro plan, and the deck has no targeted disruption for it — no blue, and nothing in white doing that job (005). The follow-up I filed is white disruption for ETB decks; that is a filed follow-up, not a change made.

Swing lethal when it is there. Both current-list games were lost with my lethal in sight: Tom closed before it resolved (004), Tom's pings got there before it landed (005). 'Sequence and close better' is my own summary of where the tuning now sits (005).

You are the archenemy from turn three and the table's answers come at you first (001). My own read at the time: that is the correct read, and the price of the plan. Still true on the current list — Oliver a turn behind all game (005).

Edgar's cast is a decision, not what happens when the mana is spare. He came down at eight in the game where the turn he landed was the turn that got Alex to 1, and the reason I gave was 'I had not even been thinking about him' (001). Turn five off Ancient Tomb is what it looks like when it goes right (005).
The refuel is what gets countered. Champion of Dusk — the draw-five that would have closed it — and Bloodthirsty Conqueror both ate counters in one game (001, on V1), and both are still in the 99.

Protection stays in hand because the mana is spent on vampires. Deflecting Swat and Teferi's Protection sat uncast for a whole game (002, on V1), and the reason that matters is the structural one: a deck that cannot afford to hold up interaction is a deck that does not run interaction, whatever the list says. Both cards are still in the 99.
Mulligan discipline. One mulligan, then kept a two-land hand out of stubbornness knowing at the time it should have gone back (002).

This pod runs heavy creature removal and heavy board wipes, and Ryan recurs artifact and enchantment removal — Anointed Procession resolved and was gone the following turn (002). It is still in the deck.
Tight lines get missed in the moment. I could have paid more life, faster, to pump the vampire and drawn a pile of extra cards off the death trigger (004).
Seat 5 in a five-player pod. My read is that the first-seat momentum advantage compounds with the mana deficit rather than just adding to it (002).

diagnosis.json says card draw is not what costs games. All three V1 games ended with vampires on board and nothing in hand (001, 002, 003), and 003 calls it 'not a new finding, it is the finding, again'. The twelve swaps were pointed at exactly that, and neither game since has ended out of gas — the engine ran off Tom's removal (004) and the board held momentum all game (005). Two games.
read.what_changed: V1 to V2 is the twelve-swap bloodline list, and 003 is where the direction was decided. After that game at Alex's the deck stopped being swarm typal and became lords and payoffs — a small number of bodies worth pumping, tokens demoted to the dig engine, white-black lifegain into lifedrain — and that note explicitly withdraws the token-conversion axis I had taken from 002. 004 and 005 are the two games on the current list. Neither ended out of gas the way the three V1 games did (001, 002, 003): in 004 the bodies dying drew cards instead of just leaving the board, and in 005 I never missed a land drop and held momentum all game. Both losses came from outside the board — a tutored two-card infinite while Edgar was dominating (004), Purphoros ETB pings before my lethal landed after I pushed tempo with Elspeth exposed (005). My own verdicts: 'the refactor really showed' (004), and after 005 that the errors are getting fewer and more specific and the tuning has moved from 'rebuild the deck' to 'sequence and close better'. Two games, so read it as an early result, not a settled one. Three older details are superseded: 001's finisher turn ran through Olivia's Wrath, 003's opener set up Warleader's Call, and my own Purphoros was in the V1 list — the swaps removed all three, so those parts of those games no longer describe the deck I am holding, and the Purphoros that beat me in 005 was Tom's commander, not a card of mine.
